passage: On the first of January, Madhuri wrote "Be healthier" on the fridge whiteboard in big green letters. Gurpreet, her flatmate, asked what that meant. "Everything," Madhuri said. "Less fried stuff, more movement, better sleep." The first week went well because she was still thinking about it every morning. Then the office moved her to the late shift, and the bus home reached after ten. Some nights she remembered the board; most nights she was too tired to decide anything and ordered the same rolls from the stall downstairs. By the second week of February the green letters had faded under a shopping list. Gurpreet asked, gently, "When were you going to do it?" Madhuri opened her mouth, then laughed. "I never actually said when."

qa.q: What did Madhuri write on the fridge whiteboard on the first of January?
qa.a: "Be healthier," in big green letters.

qa.q: Why did the resolution feel strong to Madhuri at first?
qa.a: In the first week she was still thinking about it every morning, so the goal felt alive; she had not yet seen that it depended on remembering and having energy.

qa.q: Once the late shift began, what choice could have kept the goal alive?
qa.a: Tying one concrete action to a fixed moment in the new routine, such as a short walk from the bus stop before going upstairs, so nothing depends on deciding while tired.

qa.q: How does Gurpreet see the resolution by February?
qa.a: Gurpreet watches the words fade under a shopping list and asks kindly, not critically, when it was meant to happen, which helps Madhuri spot the missing piece.

grounding: An adult makes a broad health resolution with no when or how, and it slips once tiredness and a new shift take over.

passage: "This is my year," Kishore announced at the office lunch table in Pune, spooning up dal. "Fitter, calmer, no more late-night scrolling." Gurleen, sitting across, asked which days he'd exercise. Kishore waved a hand. "Whenever I get time. I'll feel it." In January he climbed the stairs to the fourth floor instead of taking the lift, on the days he remembered. He bought a skipping rope and kept it in the car. By the end of the month the stairs happened only when the lift was broken, and the rope had slid under the car seat next to a tiffin lid. One evening in February, stuck in traffic, he found the rope while hunting for his charger and stared at it for a long time.

qa.q: Where did Kishore find the skipping rope in February?
qa.a: Under the car seat next to a tiffin lid, while hunting for his charger in traffic.

qa.q: What might Kishore have been thinking as he stared at the rope?
qa.a: He probably felt a pang of disappointment, seeing that the promise he made so confidently in January had quietly faded even though he never decided to drop it.

qa.q: Where did Kishore's plan go wrong, and what could fix it?
qa.a: "Whenever I get time" left every action to memory and mood; choosing set days and a cue, like taking the stairs every time he arrives at the office, would make it automatic.

qa.q: Why might Gurleen have asked which days?
qa.a: Gurleen seems to sense that a goal with no time attached rarely survives busy weeks, and the question was a light nudge to make it concrete.

grounding: An adult's vague resolution to get fit, with no set days or cues, drifts away by February.

passage:
"Didi, see this." Ankita held up her phone: a New Year post she had shared, "Healthier me, starting now."
Jyoti smiled. "Nice. What's the plan?"
"Just, you know, eat better, walk more. Be good."
"When's the walk?"
"Whenever. Mornings, maybe. I'll see how I feel."
Six weeks later, Jyoti found her on the sofa at eleven at night, eating chips from the packet.
"Ankita, how's the walking going?"
"Don't." Ankita pulled a cushion over her face. "I went on the fourth and the fifth. Then that deadline came, then it rained, then I just forgot it existed."
"Did you ever pick a time?"
A long pause. "No. I kept waiting to feel like it."
"Nobody feels like it at six in the morning."
"So I'm lazy?"
"No. You just left it to your mood."

qa.q: On which dates did Ankita actually go walking?
qa.a: On the fourth and the fifth.

qa.q: Why does Ankita pull a cushion over her face when Jyoti asks about the walking?
qa.a: She feels embarrassed that the plan she announced so happily has faded, and she worries it means she is lazy.

qa.q: What choice would change Ankita's next attempt?
qa.a: Picking a set time and a cue, such as walking straight after her morning tea, instead of waiting to feel like it.

qa.q: How does Jyoti see Ankita's slipping resolution?
qa.a: As her older sister, Jyoti doesn't see laziness; she notices the plan never had a time, so it depended on mood, and says so kindly.

grounding: A vague 'eat better, walk more' resolution with no time or trigger fades within weeks.

passage: I'm Sarita, and last New Year's Eve I told my flatmate Himani, very grandly, "This year I'm getting healthy." I never said what that meant. I think I pictured a new version of me who simply woke up wanting salad. For about two weeks I felt it. I walked a bit, skipped some biscuits, drank more water when I remembered. Then a big audit came at work. I stayed late, ate whatever the canteen had, and walking became something I'd do "when things settle". By February I was back to my old evenings exactly, and I hadn't even noticed the day it slipped. In March Himani asked how the healthy year was going. I laughed, but it stung. There had never been a when or a how, only a mood.

qa.q: What did Sarita tell Himani on New Year's Eve?
qa.a: Sarita said, 'This year I'm getting healthy.'

qa.q: Why did the resolution feel like it was working for Sarita in the first two weeks?
qa.a: The New Year mood carried it; Sarita felt motivated and still remembered the goal, so a concrete plan didn't seem necessary.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could Sarita try instead?
qa.a: Nothing tied the goal to a time or cue, so the audit pushed it aside; Sarita could pick one action linked to a moment, like a walk straight after getting home on set days.

qa.q: What might Himani have noticed before asking in March?
qa.a: Himani had probably seen the old evenings return and asked as a gentle check-in, perhaps not realising the laugh covered a sting.

grounding: An adult makes a vague resolution to get healthy with no timing or method and slides back to old habits by February.

Jeevan signed up on 2 January, full of energy. When I asked what he wanted, he said, "To be healthier, generally. Better food, more movement, all of it." I asked which days he'd come. "Whenever I can. I'll just feel it." He came three Saturdays running. Then his sister's wedding preparations started, then a work trip, and I haven't seen him since the last week of January. Today I met him at the vegetable stall. He said, a bit sheepishly, that he was "back to the old routine" and didn't know when it happened. Next time someone joins, I'll ask for one fixed class and what comes right before it. "Whenever" seems to depend on how the week feels.

qa.a: He came three Saturdays running.

qa.q: What does Jeevan's sheepishness at the vegetable stall suggest?
qa.a: He seems embarrassed; he still cares about the goal and hadn't noticed it slipping away, so meeting Rashmi brought it back to mind.

passage: Pallavi, you're asking how I stay so regular with my walks? Sit, let me tell you about the year I did not. I was twenty-four then, your Manjula aunty, working at the bank in Mysuru. On the first of January I told my roommate Revathi, "This year I'll be healthier." That was all. No time, no place. I bought a yoga mat and felt wonderful for a week. Then came the audit. Some mornings I was tired, some evenings it rained, some days I just didn't feel like it. Each day I thought, I'll start properly tomorrow. By February the mat was rolled up under the cot with dust on it, and I was eating fried snacks at the tea shop again. Revathi never teased me, but she stopped asking. It was only the next year, when I said "after the bus drops me, I walk around the lake," that anything stuck.

qa.q: What did Manjula buy after making her resolution?
qa.a: She bought a yoga mat.

qa.q: How did young Manjula feel when she kept saying she would start properly tomorrow?
qa.a: She likely felt hopeful and sure she meant it each day, which is why the vague goal felt reasonable, but it left her depending on her mood, so she drifted and probably felt quietly disappointed by February.

qa.q: At what point in the story could Manjula have changed course, and how?
qa.a: In January, instead of just saying 'be healthier', she could have tied a clear action to a set moment, like walking after the bus drop, which is what finally worked the next year.

qa.q: How might Revathi have felt watching the mat gather dust?
qa.a: Revathi may have felt awkward or unsure whether to mention it, so she stopped asking to avoid hurting Manjula.

grounding: It shows an adult whose resolution to be healthier had no when or how, so she slid back into old habits by February.

passage: Trisha wrote it on the whiteboard of the flat on New Year's morning: EAT BETTER. MOVE MORE. Madhav, her flatmate, added a smiley. Then the night-shift rota at the call centre changed. Some weeks she started at nine at night, some at eleven, and the canteen shut at midnight. Whenever she remembered the whiteboard, she was either asleep or on a break with ten minutes and a vending machine. "I'll plan it when the rota settles," she told Madhav in the third week. It didn't settle. On the first Sunday of February, Madhav found her at the counter with a cup of instant noodles at four in the afternoon, her breakfast. The whiteboard still said MOVE MORE, the letters faded where her sleeve had brushed them. "I did mean it," she said, not looking up. "I just never decided what it actually meant on a Tuesday night."

qa.q: What did Trisha write on the whiteboard on New Year's morning?
qa.a: She wrote EAT BETTER. MOVE MORE.

qa.q: What was Trisha feeling when she said she never decided what the goal meant on a Tuesday night?
qa.a: She sounds disappointed and a bit ashamed, avoiding Madhav's eyes, while realising the goal failed because it never said when or how.

qa.q: What small step could Trisha try that fits her shifting rota?
qa.a: She could tie an action to a cue that stays the same on any shift, such as packing a proper meal right after she wakes up, instead of waiting for the rota to settle.

qa.q: How might Madhav feel seeing the faded whiteboard and the noodles?
qa.a: Madhav might feel sympathetic and unsure whether to say anything, since he had cheered the goal on New Year's morning.

grounding: It shows an adult whose vague resolution, made without a when or how and squeezed by shift work, faded back into old routines by February.

passage: "So, still on the healthy year?" Bhavna asked, holding the lift door on the fourth floor of their Hyderabad office. Afreen laughed and stepped in. On January first she had announced it at Bhavna's rooftop party: this year, I'm getting healthier. Everyone had clapped. In the first week she had taken the stairs twice and gone to bed early once. After that the days just filled up. Some nights she scrolled until one, some mornings she grabbed a samosa from the canteen because she was running late. None of it felt like breaking a promise, because the promise had never said anything specific. Now it was the second week of February, and she was in the lift again. "I'm still on it," Afreen said. "Sort of." As the lift climbed, she tried to name one thing she had actually changed and couldn't find one.

qa.q: Where did Afreen announce her plan to get healthier?
qa.a: She announced it at Bhavna's rooftop party on January first.

qa.q: Why didn't Afreen feel she was breaking a promise when she scrolled late or grabbed a samosa?
qa.a: Because the promise never said anything specific, each slip felt harmless; by February she felt uneasy and a little embarrassed when she couldn't name one real change.

qa.q: What would you advise Afreen to try instead of 'getting healthier'?
qa.a: Pick one specific action tied to a clear cue, for example taking the stairs whenever she arrives at the office, so it happens without needing mood or memory.

qa.q: What would change if Afreen had said 'I take the stairs every morning' at the party?
qa.a: She would have a clear moment each day to act and to notice a slip, and Bhavna could have asked about something concrete instead of a vague goal.

grounding: It shows an adult whose resolution to be healthier said nothing about when or how, so ordinary busy days pulled her back to old habits by February.

“Aparna, is that a new gym bag?”
“It was new in January, Devika. Now it's a very expensive laundry basket.”
“What happened to ‘healthier this year’?”
“It happened for two weeks. I ate salads. I walked a bit. Then…”
“Then?”
“Then work got busy, and I'd think ‘I'll start again Monday.’ And Monday I wouldn't remember, or I'd be tired, or it was raining.”
“Did you ever decide when you'd walk? Like, what time?”
“No. Just… more.”
“More when?”
Aparna laughed, a little embarrassed. “More whenever I felt like it. Which was never.”
Devika pointed at the calendar. “It's the ninth of February.”
“I know. I was so determined on the first of January.” Aparna stared at the bag. “I think determination was all I had.”

passage:
On 1 January I wrote “Get healthier” in big letters on my whiteboard. I'm Vaibhav, twenty-four, and I really meant it.
I didn't write anything else. No time, no plan. I just thought, I'll eat better and move more.
In the first week I had fruit for breakfast and took the stairs twice. Then there was a deadline at work, then my cousin's wedding, then a cold. Each time I thought I'd get back to it. I never picked a day.
By February, my breakfast was two samosas from the stall under the office again. I noticed the whiteboard one evening, still saying “Get healthier,” and felt a mix of guilt and annoyance.
My colleague Ishita, who cycles every morning at 6:30 without fail, once told me, “I don't decide. It's just what happens after my alarm.”
That's what I was missing. A “when.”

qa.q: What did Vaibhav write on the whiteboard?
qa.a: Vaibhav wrote “Get healthier” in big letters.

qa.q: How did Vaibhav feel seeing the whiteboard in February?
qa.a: Vaibhav felt guilty and annoyed, since the resolution had quietly drifted away.

qa.q: What could Vaibhav try, based on Ishita's example?
qa.a: Link a specific healthy action to a fixed cue and time, like cycling right after the alarm.

qa.q: How might Ishita see resolutions like Vaibhav's?
qa.a: Ishita probably sees that without a set time they depend on mood, which is why Ishita's own routine doesn't need decisions.

grounding: The reflection shows an adult resolving to be healthier without saying when or how, and drifting back to old habits by February.

passage:
Yoga teacher's note, beginners' batch, 12 February.
In January we had twenty-two new students. Today we had nine.
Gargi was one of the most enthusiastic in January. She said she wanted “to get fitter this year.” Asked which days she'd come, she said, “Whenever I can.” She attended six classes in January, none in February.
Her friend Sunaina joined the same week and said, “Tuesday and Thursday, 7 a.m., straight after I drop my son at the bus.” She has not missed a class.
Both seemed equally determined. One had a when and a cue.
When I called Gargi yesterday, she sounded embarrassed. I told her it wasn't a character flaw; the plan was simply vague.
What I did next: I suggested she choose two fixed class times attached to something she already does, and she chose Monday and Wednesday after her morning tea. She is booked for Monday.

qa.q: How many classes did Gargi attend in February?
qa.a: She attended none in February.

qa.q: How did Gargi feel when the teacher called?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed, as if the lapse were a personal failure rather than a vague plan.

qa.q: What did the teacher suggest, and why could it help?
qa.a: Choosing two fixed class times attached to her morning tea, so coming doesn't depend on memory and mood.

qa.q: How might Sunaina see her own routine compared with Gargi's?
qa.a: Sunaina probably feels steady and matter-of-fact about it, since her classes are tied to dropping her son at the bus.

grounding: The yoga teacher's note shows an adult's vague resolution fading by February, while a friend with a set time and cue keeps going.

passage:
3 February
Healthier this year. That's what I wrote on 1 January in big letters on the first page of this diary. I, Indu, twenty-four, was going to be a new person.
Let's see. Week one I walked twice in the morning. Week two it was cold. Week three there was the audit, and Darshan kept bringing samosas to the office at four, and I kept eating them. By week four I had forgotten the resolution existed until I opened this diary today.
Healthier how? When? I never wrote any of that. Every morning I woke up and decided depending on how I felt, and most mornings I felt sleepy.
It's annoying that the page still looks so confident. I feel a bit silly. I think "healthier" needs a time and a place, or it's just a nice word.

qa.q: What did Darshan keep bringing to the office at four?
qa.a: Darshan kept bringing samosas.

qa.q: How does Indu feel reading the resolution page on 3 February?
qa.a: Indu feels a bit silly and annoyed, because the confident page contrasts with a month of drifting back to old habits.

qa.q: What could Indu change to make the resolution work?
qa.a: Indu could turn it into something specific with a when and where, like walking at seven on weekday mornings, instead of deciding by mood each day.

qa.q: How might Darshan see the samosa habit?
qa.a: Darshan probably sees it as a friendly office treat and has no idea it is undoing Indu's resolution.

grounding: It shows an adult whose vague resolution to be healthier had no when or how and faded by February because it depended on memory and mood.

On New Year's night in Hoshangabad, Eshaan stood on the roof with his friends and announced, "This year, I'm going to be healthy." Everyone cheered and ate more gajar halwa.
For the first week he woke early, felt proud, and walked by the river. Then the school where he taught started exam duties. Some mornings he remembered the resolution; most mornings he remembered it at eleven, in the staffroom, with a plate of pakoras in front of him.
In the second week of February, his friend Chaitanya asked, "So, healthy man, how's it going?"
Eshaan laughed, but it came out flat. "I don't even know. What does healthy mean? I never decided."
"When were you supposed to walk?"
"Whenever I felt like it."
Chaitanya just raised his eyebrows. Eshaan looked at the pakoras and pushed the plate away, then pulled it back.

On the first of January, in their flat in Leeds with frost on the windows, Abebe announced over leftover injera, "This is the year I get healthier." Nkechi raised her mug. "How?"
"Just... healthier. Better food. More moving. You'll see."
For the first week he took the stairs twice and bought a bag of apples. Then the dark evenings came, the office got busy, and "healthier" had no time and no place attached to it. Some nights he remembered at eleven, lying on the sofa, and felt vaguely bad. Most nights he didn't remember at all.
By February the apples had gone soft in the bowl. Abebe noticed them one Sunday while ordering fried chicken. "I really meant it," he told Nkechi, puzzled. "I don't know where it went."

qa.a: A bag of apples.

qa.q: How does Abebe feel in February?

qa.q: What could make Abebe's goal hold?
